articles.headline: Inflation and Fed Policy Are on Collision Course, Page Says
articles.summary: T. Rowe Price CIO Sébastien Page stated on Bloomberg Surveillance that the primary risk in financial markets is a 'collision course between inflation and Fed policy.' This comes as Jerome Powell's term as Fed Chair ended May 15, with the U.S. Senate confirming Kevin Warsh as his successor. Warsh is viewed as more open to rate cuts, but persistent inflation data has made near-term Fed rate cuts unlikely.

articles.headline: Inflation Rate Projected to Hit 6% in the Second Quarter, Top Economic Forecasters Say
articles.summary: The Survey of Professional Forecasters — a blue-ribbon group polled each quarter by the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia — projected consumer price inflation to hit 6% in Q2 2026. The projection comes amid an ongoing energy price shock tied to geopolitical conflict and persistent supply disruptions. The forecast reinforces growing concerns that inflationary pressures are becoming more entrenched, complicating the Federal Reserve's efforts to guide inflation back to its 2% target.

articles.headline: U.S. Retail Sales Rise in April Despite Inflation and Higher Energy Costs
articles.summary: The U.S. Census Bureau's Advance Monthly Retail Trade Survey for April 2026 showed retail and food services sales of $757.1 billion, up 0.5% from March and up 4.9% from April 2025. Retail trade sales were up 5.2% year-over-year, and nonstore retailers—the e-commerce proxy—rose 11.1% from a year ago. Total sales for the February–April 2026 period were up 4.4% from the same period a year ago, while food services and drinking places were up 2.7% from April 2025.

articles.headline: New Sales and Inventory Numbers Reflect Cautious Consumers and Retailers
articles.summary: New retail sales and wholesale inventory data show consumers growing more cautious as inflation accelerates, with the nominal retail sales increase reflecting higher prices rather than more units sold. Some wholesalers are building inventories in anticipation of further fuel cost increases, while demand for big-ticket items such as cars and furniture is softening. Supply chain management experts noted wholesalers are front-loading purchases ahead of back-to-school and holiday seasons to lock in current prices before further inflation.

articles.headline: Retail Q1 2026: Low Availability and Construction Slow Absorption
articles.summary: Q1 2026 retail market reports from CBRE, JLL, Newmark, and others showed negative net absorption across nearly all tracked reports, driven by a wave of store closures from multiple bankruptcy filings adding available space to the market. Consumer sentiment was negatively affected by lingering inflation, uncertainty about the job market, and the impact of the Iran conflict on fuel costs, per Newmark analysts, though retail sales and consumer spending remained in positive territory. Sun Belt markets outpaced the rest of the country in retail metrics driven by population growth, and JLL noted that for the remainder of 2026, performance will depend more on which markets a portfolio is in than on national averages.

articles.headline: House Cuts Build-To-Rent Ban From Latest Bill, Targets Vote Next Week
articles.summary: The House removed a ban on build-to-rent housing from its latest legislative package and is targeting a vote the following week on the modified bill, after President Trump publicly pushed House members to pass a housing bill that had included a forced-sale provision for BTR properties. The real estate lobby had sounded the alarm over the forced-sale provision in the original bill, arguing it would chill investment in single-family rental development. The modified bill's passage timeline remains uncertain pending negotiations among House members.

articles.headline: Hapag-Lloyd Q1 2026 Loss: Strait of Hormuz Chaos and Weak Freight Rates Hit Shipping
articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd reported a Q1 2026 net loss of €219 million ($257 million), compared to a profit of €446 million in Q1 2025, as lower freight rates and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted global shipping operations. Average freight rates fell 9.5% year-over-year to $1,330 per TEU, and hundreds of commercial vessels carrying up to 20,000 seafarers remained unable to transit the Strait since the U.S. and Israel began attacks on Iran in late February 2026. Brent crude prices nearly doubled during the quarter, ending March at $118.35 per barrel, while low-sulfur bunker fuel prices surged more than 80% from year-end 2025 levels. The company maintained its full-year 2026 EBITDA guidance of $1.1 billion to $3.1 billion but warned the outlook remains subject to 'considerable uncertainty.'

articles.headline: Traders Now See Next Fed Interest Rate Move as a Hike Following Inflation Surge
articles.summary: Following a week of hotter-than-expected inflation readings, fed funds futures traders are now pricing in a Federal Reserve interest rate hike as soon as December 2026, the first time in the current cycle markets have priced in a hike rather than a cut. A December hike carries a nearly 51% probability, January a 60% probability, and March better than 71%, per CME Group's FedWatch tool. The Survey of Professional Forecasters released Friday projects Q2 consumer price inflation to hit 6%, a dramatic revision from the prior 2.7% estimate, driven largely by energy prices tied to the Iran conflict and the Strait of Hormuz. Incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, confirmed by the Senate Wednesday, inherits an increasingly complicated inflation picture as GDP growth is simultaneously revised down to 2.2% for the full year.

articles.headline: Treasury Yields Surge as Inflation Data Points to Tricky Rates Path for New Fed Chair Warsh
articles.summary: U.S. Treasury yields spiked Friday following a week of elevated inflation data, with the 10-year note surging nearly 14 basis points to 4.595% and the 30-year bond jumping to just over 5.1%, its highest level since May 2025. The 2-year yield rose close to 9 basis points to 4.079%. Import prices rose 1.9% in April and 4.2% on a 12-month basis — the largest annual gain since October 2022 — while export prices surged 8.8%, the highest since September 2022, as Middle East conflict keeps energy prices elevated. West Texas Intermediate crude rose to $104.39 per barrel, up $3.22, after the Trump-Xi summit concluded with little to show on energy diplomacy.

articles.headline: Bonds, Stocks and Precious Metals Slump as Inflation Fears Mount, Silver Falls 7%
articles.summary: Global government bonds, precious metals, and international stocks sold off Friday as inflation fears intensified and President Trump concluded a three-day visit to China with no meaningful agreement on energy or trade. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest level in nearly a year at 4.544%, while money markets priced in a near-zero chance of any Fed rate cuts this year and a 50% chance of a December hike, per CME FedWatch. Silver fell 7% on the session. The combination of Iran war energy shocks, ongoing tariff uncertainty, and political upheaval in the U.K. weighed on cross-asset sentiment globally.

articles.headline: Global Bond Selloff Worsens as Rising Oil Prices Spook Investors
articles.summary: Global government bond markets fell sharply on May 15, with US 10-year Treasury yields rising 12 basis points to 4.6% and 30-year yields approaching 5.12%—the highest since 2007—as Brent crude climbed past $107 per barrel amid an unresolved Strait of Hormuz standoff following the Iran war. The selloff was compounded by back-to-back US government reports showing consumer and wholesale prices accelerating at the fastest pace since 2022, with traders now pricing a near two-thirds probability of a Fed rate hike in December. Incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, narrowly confirmed by the Senate this week, faces the selloff as his first major test. The S&P 500 fell more than 1% on Friday, pulling back from a recent rally, while gas prices nationally held above $4.50 per gallon—up 51% since the Iran war began.

articles.headline: Companies Are Getting Tariff Refunds. Here's What They Plan to Do With the Money.
articles.summary: The US Customs and Border Protection began processing the first wave of electronic tariff refunds on May 12, returning billions of dollars to importers who paid levies later struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2026. CBP said about 15% of submitted claims were rejected due to incorrect information or ineligible shipments. Major companies including General Motors said they expect hundreds of millions of dollars in refunds; Citi analysis found Walmart is owed approximately $10 billion, Target $2 billion, and Nike $1 billion. Companies have stated plans to use refunds to pay down debt, rehire workers, restock inventory, or potentially lower prices, while consumers are not directly eligible for refunds.

articles.headline: The New Route Around Hormuz Involves a Massive Convoy of Trucks
articles.summary: With the Strait of Hormuz closed following the outbreak of war in Iran, shippers and logistics operators have developed an alternative overland route using massive truck convoys to move energy and cargo around the conflict zone. The closure of the strait has driven Brent crude above $107 per barrel, up more than 10% this week alone, creating severe cost pressure across global supply chains. Trump-Xi summit talks in Beijing this week failed to produce breakthroughs on reopening the strait, with China calling for rapid reopening but no concrete agreement reached. The alternative convoy route adds significant transit time and cost compared to the standard maritime passage.

articles.headline: US Shopping Data Is Good, But Something Worrisome Is Lurking
articles.summary: Bloomberg's Retail Monitor reported that US retail sales data this week showed surface-level strength in consumer spending, but that rising oil prices above $105 per barrel and surging bond yields are creating a worrisome undercurrent for forward consumer demand. Producer price data released this week showed costs accelerating at the fastest pace since 2022, signaling potential margin compression for retailers and goods distributors. The inflation pressures stem from the combined effect of the Strait of Hormuz closure and ongoing tariff-related cost pass-through still working through supply chains. Analysts noted the combination of high gas prices—nationally averaging $4.50 per gallon—and tightening financial conditions presents a risk to the consumer spending outlook in the coming months.

articles.headline: Supreme Court Rules Unanimously: Freight Broker C.H. Robinson Faces Negligent Hiring Lawsuit
articles.summary: The US Supreme Court ruled unanimously this week that freight broker C.H. Robinson can face a state-law negligent hiring lawsuit from plaintiff Shawn Montgomery, rejecting the argument that federal law shields brokers from such claims. The ruling found that plaintiffs can bring state-law negligent hiring claims against freight brokers, removing a key legal protection the industry had relied upon. Industry analysts noted the ruling is expected to raise insurance premiums across the brokerage sector, tighten carrier vetting standards, and increase barriers to entry for new brokers. Over time, tighter carrier qualification standards are expected to reduce available capacity and place upward pressure on freight rates.

articles.headline: Perfectus Aluminum and Related Companies Agree to Pay $549.5M to Settle False Claims Act Allegations Relating to Evaded Customs Duties
articles.summary: Perfectus Aluminum Inc. and affiliated companies agreed to pay $549.5 million to settle False Claims Act allegations that they evaded customs duties on aluminum imports, in one of the largest customs fraud settlements in US history. The case involved allegations of tariff evasion through misclassification of aluminum products to avoid anti-dumping and countervailing duties. The settlement signals intensified federal enforcement of customs compliance as part of the broader crackdown on tariff evasion following the Supreme Court's ruling on IEEPA tariffs. Importers, freight brokers, and 3PLs are expected to face heightened customs scrutiny as a result of the case.

articles.headline: Amazon Rolls Out 30-Minute Delivery on Thousands of Groceries and Essentials
articles.summary: Amazon launched a 30-minute delivery service covering thousands of grocery and everyday essentials items, expanding its ultra-fast fulfillment capabilities to a broader product set beyond its existing same-day offerings. The service relies on Amazon's network of urban micro-fulfillment nodes and delivery infrastructure. The rollout follows Amazon's May 4 launch of Amazon Supply Chain Services (ASCS), which opened its full logistics network to third-party businesses. The 30-minute delivery expansion intensifies pressure on traditional grocery retailers and last-mile delivery providers, and requires continued investment in dense, last-mile warehouse infrastructure.

articles.headline: project44 Launches Autopilot to Cut Freight Costs, Improve Data Quality, Optimize Inventory Levels, and Accelerate Cash Flow
articles.summary: Supply chain visibility platform project44 launched 'Autopilot,' an AI-driven tool designed to autonomously cut freight costs, improve shipment data quality, optimize inventory levels, and accelerate cash flow for shippers and logistics operators. The system uses machine learning to make automated decisions across freight procurement, routing, and inventory positioning without requiring manual intervention from supply chain teams. The launch comes as shippers face elevated freight costs due to oil price spikes from the Strait of Hormuz closure and continued tariff-related supply chain disruptions. project44 positions Autopilot as a response to the growing complexity of operating supply chains in a volatile trade and energy environment.

articles.headline: The Energy Crisis Is Becoming a Currency Crisis in Asia's Emerging Markets
articles.summary: Bloomberg Opinion reports that the Iran conflict-driven energy price shock is spreading into a currency crisis across Asian emerging markets, with major energy importers including the Philippine peso, South Korean won, Thai baht, and Egyptian pound among the worst-performing currencies since the start of the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran. The supply-side energy shock has spread into food systems, financial markets, and regional economies, raising concerns about stagflation. India has asked the U.S. to extend its waiver on Russian oil cargo sales beyond the May 16 expiry date. The disruption is affecting global shipping routes, container costs, and supply chain reliability.

articles.headline: Construction Material Costs Rose 6.2% Through April, Pressuring CRE Projects
articles.summary: Construction material costs rose 6.2% through April 2026, with energy, steel, and lumber prices climbing and pressuring commercial real estate development projects across the country. As of April 2026, steel, aluminum, and copper items carry a 50% tariff, with derivatives at 25% and industrial/electrical equipment incorporating those materials facing a 15% tariff. Associated Builders and Contractors data shows nonresidential construction input prices surged at a 12.6% annualized rate during the first two months of 2026, the fastest pace since the supply chain disruptions of early 2022. The industry needs approximately 349,000 net new workers in 2026 beyond normal hiring levels to maintain supply-demand equilibrium, with the shortage described as structural rather than cyclical.

articles.headline: Starbucks Announces Third Round of U.S. Layoffs, 300 Corporate Employees Cut
articles.summary: Starbucks announced it will lay off 300 U.S. corporate employees in its third round of job cuts as part of its ongoing turnaround strategy under CEO Brian Niccol. The coffee giant is also closing some regional support offices, with combined severance costs and office space reassessment expected to result in $400 million in restructuring charges. Starbucks expects to record $280 million in noncash charges tied to asset impairments and $120 million in cash charges related to the layoffs. This follows an earlier round that cut 1,100 jobs and another that eliminated 900 nonretail positions as part of a $1 billion restructuring plan.

articles.headline: Xi and Trump Map Out a New Framework
articles.summary: President Trump concluded his visit to Beijing with Xi Jinping, announcing deals and a new strategic framework for the US-China economic relationship. The summit addressed a range of economic and geopolitical issues including trade tensions, tariff levels, semiconductors, and AI. The current US-China trade status quo is set to expire in November, creating urgency around the talks. Analysts noted that while the optics were positive, major sticking points remained unresolved.

articles.headline: ITS Logistics May Port/Rail Ramp Freight Index: Strait of Hormuz Closure Sends Fuel Shock Through Supply Chains
articles.summary: ITS Logistics released its May Port/Rail Ramp Freight Index reporting elevated status across Atlantic and Gulf port regions, with container termination challenges at key West Coast gateways. The ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz is pushing fuel costs higher, with retail diesel reaching $5.639 per gallon as of May 11—a jump of nearly 29 cents since the end of April. FTR Transportation Intelligence reported spot market rates approached all-time highs during the week of May 8, driven by fuel cost pass-through and tightening capacity. The Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance's annual International Roadcheck began May 12, with an out-of-service rate of 31.4% further tightening trucking capacity.

articles.headline: Starbucks Plans First Corporate Tech Office in India to Cut Costs
articles.summary: Starbucks Corp. announced plans to open a technology office in India as part of a broader initiative to cut $2 billion in costs. The new hub is slated for the company's fiscal year 2027, which begins in October, according to an internal message seen by Bloomberg News. The India location will be Starbucks' first corporate office in the country, and the company expects to begin recruiting once a site is selected later this year.

articles.headline: Fed Names Powell Chair Pro Tempore Until Warsh Sworn In
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve named Jerome Powell as temporary chair of the Board of Governors until his successor Kevin Warsh is officially sworn in, according to a central bank statement released Friday. Some board members issued a statement opposing the action, saying 'we do not support an unlimited timeframe for temporary chair designation.' The transition marks a leadership change at the Fed as Warsh prepares to assume the role of Federal Reserve Chair.

articles.headline: NextEra Energy Is Said to Be in Talks to Acquire Dominion
articles.summary: NextEra Energy Inc. is in discussions to acquire Dominion Energy Inc. in a mostly stock deal, according to a person familiar with the matter. A transaction could be announced as soon as Monday, though no agreement has been reached and talks could still end without one. The combined company would have an enterprise value of approximately $400 billion including debt. The deal is driven by surging electricity demand from AI data centers, industrial reshoring, and electrification, and would expand NextEra's reach into the PJM Interconnection grid, which extends from Washington to Chicago and encompasses Northern Virginia's data center cluster.

articles.headline: Boeing Wins 200-Jet Plane Order From China, Trump Says
articles.summary: President Trump announced that China agreed to purchase 200 Boeing commercial jets, marking Boeing's first major aircraft sale to China in nearly a decade, coming out of Trump's summit with President Xi Jinping in Beijing. Trump stated China reserved the right to buy up to 750 aircraft total, though neither the Chinese government nor Boeing issued a confirming statement. Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg accompanied Trump on the trip; analysts had expected an order of up to 500 aircraft. Boeing shares fell 4.73% on Thursday following the announcement, which fell short of Jefferies' estimate of a 500-plane deal.

articles.headline: Brent Crude Rises Above $109 Per Barrel as Strait of Hormuz Remains Effectively Closed
articles.summary: Brent crude futures rose past $109 per barrel on May 15 and posted an 8.1% weekly gain as the Strait of Hormuz remained effectively closed amid stalled US-Iran peace talks. The IEA reported crude and fuel flows through the Strait dropped by approximately 4 million barrels per day in March and April, warning the global oil market could remain materially undersupplied through October even if the conflict resolves next month. President Trump warned Iran to reach a deal or face 'annihilation,' while Iran reported around 30 ships had crossed the Strait since Wednesday. WTI crude oil was trading near $106 per barrel, up over 60% since late February, with the national average gasoline price at $4.53 per gallon.

articles.headline: US Industrial Production Rose 0.7% in April, Strongest Gain in 14 Months
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve released its G.17 report on May 15, showing US industrial production increased 0.7% in April 2026, the largest monthly gain in 14 months and well above the consensus estimate of 0.3%. Manufacturing output, which accounts for approximately 78% of total industrial production, rose 0.6%, beating forecasts of 0.2%. Capacity utilization moved up to 76.1%, still 3.3 percentage points below its long-run average. Utilities output increased 1.9%, while mining output edged down 0.1%.

articles.headline: NY Empire State Manufacturing Index Surges to 19.6 in May, Highest Level Since April 2022
articles.source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York / Bloomberg
articles.summary: The New York Fed's Empire State Manufacturing Index jumped to 19.6 in May 2026, far exceeding the consensus estimate of 7.0 and up from 11 in April, marking the highest reading in more than four years. New orders rose to 22.7 and shipments to 18.9, with employment levels and average workweek both continuing to increase. Delivery times lengthened substantially to 20.4, and supply availability worsened, while input price increases accelerated sharply to 62.6, up from 51 the prior month. Firms grew more optimistic about the six-month outlook, with the forward-looking index rising to 33.5 from 19.6.

articles.headline: IEA Warns Global Oil Market Could Remain Severely Undersupplied Through October Even If Iran Conflict Ends
articles.summary: The International Energy Agency issued a warning this week that the global oil market could remain materially undersupplied through October 2026, even if the Iran conflict resolves next month. Crude and fuel flows through the Strait of Hormuz dropped by approximately 4 million barrels per day in March and April due to the effective closure of the waterway. The IEA, shipping companies, Amazon, FedEx, and USPS have all implemented fuel surcharges in response to the ongoing energy crisis. A Goldman Sachs survey found a majority of investors expect disruptions beyond the end of June, with 43% not expecting shipping to normalize until after July.

articles.headline: Connect CRE: AI and CRE — Industry Moving Cautiously, Prioritizing Explainability and Auditability
articles.summary: A joint study by First American Data and DealGround found that AI adoption in commercial real estate is proceeding cautiously, with firms prioritizing explainability, provenance, and defensible outputs over full automation. The study noted that many CRE workflows depend on fragmented historical data, unstructured documents, and legacy systems where small inaccuracies can create significant operational or financial consequences. AI and automation were identified as the leading catalysts for change in corporate real estate portfolio management, but actual implementation remains a work in progress. The study concluded that the market is 'pressure-testing whether current AI systems can consistently produce reliable, auditable outputs.'

articles.headline: Global Inventory Race Intensifies in Shadow of the Iran War
articles.summary: Bloomberg reports that companies globally are accelerating inventory stockpiling driven by uncertainty from the ongoing Iran war and its impact on oil supplies and shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz. The inventory buildup reflects fears of supply chain disruption as the Hormuz standoff drags on, with businesses seeking to insulate operations from potential shortages. The race to build safety stock is creating near-term demand for warehouse and storage space across multiple sectors.

articles.headline: How a CEO and Trump Donor Is Weaponizing Tariffs Against His Rivals
articles.summary: Cambria, the top U.S. manufacturer of quartz countertops, has pursued a tariff petition that resulted in the U.S. International Trade Commission recommending tariffs of up to 40% on imported quartz slabs for a four-year period, plus import quotas. The recommendation now goes to President Trump for a final decision, with the trade commission expected to send recommendations to the president by Monday. MS International, a large California-based distributor of quartz and home-design materials claiming approximately $2.5 billion in annual sales, organized opposition to the petition, calling it an action by a small number of corporations pitted against thousands of fabricators, distributors, retailers, and American workers. Updated May 17, 2026.

articles.headline: Stock Market Today (May 18, 2026): Stock Futures Down After Record-Setting Week
articles.summary: U.S. stock futures fell Monday morning as investors monitored the U.S.-Iran conflict and prepared for Nvidia and Target earnings later in the week. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 0.85% to $106.30 a barrel, while Brent crude gained 0.89% to $110.20 a barrel. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq had hit fresh record highs the prior week, while the Dow briefly reclaimed the 50,000 level. Iran sent an amended set of ceasefire terms to the Trump administration via Pakistani mediators while President Trump warned the "clock is ticking."

articles.headline: G-7 Finance Chiefs Confront Bond Selloff as Inflation Risks Dominate Talks
articles.summary: G-7 finance ministers meeting in Paris were confronted by a deepening global bond selloff driven by investor fears over oil-fueled inflation tied to the ongoing US-Iran conflict and the Strait of Hormuz closure. Talks meant to address structural economic imbalances — including the US budget deficit and China's weak consumption — were overshadowed by spiking yields across sovereign debt markets. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Bloomberg Television that the bond market is "correcting, but I wouldn't go as far as to say it's collapsing." The 30-year US yield was the most elevated since 2007 and German 30-year debt hit its loftiest level in 15 years.

articles.headline: Global Bond Yields at Multiyear Highs on Mounting Inflation Risk
articles.summary: Global bond yields hovered near multiyear highs on Monday as rising energy prices stoked inflation concerns, with 30-year US yields hitting their highest level since 2007. Japanese government bonds notched the biggest losses, with the 30-year yield surging to its highest since that maturity was first sold in 1999. The selloff followed Friday's rout, when the S&P 500 dropped more than 1% as global yields jumped. The US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to approximately 4.63%, its highest since January 2025, as ongoing deadlock over the Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz closure continued to fuel inflation expectations.

articles.headline: Bond Rout Deepens as Rising Oil Prices Stoke Inflation Fears
articles.summary: A rout in global bonds intensified on May 18 as the deadlock over the Iran war pushed Brent crude above $111 a barrel and deepened inflation fears, with stocks extending their slide. WTI crude oil futures climbed back toward $107 per barrel as uncertainty deepened over US-Iran negotiations aimed at reopening the key Strait of Hormuz. Traders are now fully pricing in one rate hike by the Federal Reserve by March next year, with more than a 50% chance that interest rates will rise before the end of 2026. The latest US CPI and PPI reports indicated the energy price shock is feeding into broader US inflation, prompting markets to rule out any Fed rate cuts this year.

articles.headline: Yield Surge Puts Logic Behind Stocks Rally to the Test
articles.summary: Bloomberg's Markets Daily newsletter on May 18 reported signs that even a surge in bond yields may not be enough to derail the stock rally built on AI optimism. The S&P 500 dropped more than 1% on Friday as global yields jumped, and markets looked weak again overnight. Index futures pared losses in the European trading session as the bond selloff eased. Investors are monitoring the upcoming FOMC meeting minutes and flash US PMI data for further direction on monetary policy.

articles.headline: Strategists Say Soaring Japanese Bond Yields Show Fiscal Worries
articles.summary: Japanese government bonds sold off sharply on Monday, sending yields to record highs as rising oil prices fueled inflation fears, with the 10-year yield rising to approximately 2.80%. Producer prices in Japan increased 4.9% in April, accelerating sharply from 2.9% in March and surpassing market forecasts, amid intensifying cost pressures following the surge in energy prices tied to the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Bank of Japan board member Kazuyuki Masu called for policy rates to be raised as soon as possible, warning of increasingly persistent inflation risks stemming from the conflict. Bloomberg strategists noted the selloff reflects deepening fiscal concerns beyond just energy inflation.

articles.headline: Gold Holds Decline as Hormuz Quagmire Keeps Inflation Fears High
articles.summary: Gold held a decline on May 18 as a lack of progress in reopening the Strait of Hormuz continued to fan inflation concerns that have sent bond markets tumbling. The Strait has been largely closed since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28, 2026, blocking roughly 20% of the world's seaborne oil trade. Trump warned Iran to 'get moving' after departing China without securing meaningful progress toward ending the conflict or reopening the strait. Energy infrastructure across the Persian Gulf came under renewed attack over the weekend, including a nuclear facility in the UAE, adding to supply disruption fears.

articles.headline: NextEra to Buy Dominion for $67 Billion to Form Power Giant
articles.summary: NextEra Energy Inc. agreed to pay approximately $67 billion in stock for Dominion Energy Inc. in the biggest power acquisition ever, creating a giant utility extending from Florida to the data center corridor in Virginia. The deal would give NextEra a swathe of electricity assets across Virginia and the Carolinas and position it as a dominant utility in a region struggling to meet surging demand from newly built artificial intelligence facilities. The combined company would serve approximately 10 million utility customer accounts, own 110 gigawatts of generation, and become the world leader in renewables and battery storage. The deal is expected to close in 12 to 18 months, pending approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, state regulators, and the Justice Department.

articles.headline: Ford Bets on Bronco SUV to Revive Flagging European Sales
articles.summary: Ford Motor Co. announced plans to revive its struggling European passenger car business by building a compact Bronco SUV at its Valencia, Spain plant starting in 2028, as part of a product offensive involving five new European models by 2029. Ford will also introduce smaller electric and combustion-engine vehicles for Europe to compete with an influx of less expensive Chinese brands. Ford Pro's paid software subscriptions grew 30% year-over-year to 879,000 in Q1 2026, with gross margins above 50%, reflecting the company's pivot toward software-and-services revenue. Ford also called on the EU to align emissions regulations with consumer demand and available charging infrastructure.

articles.headline: Ford Bets on Bronco SUV to Revive Flagging European Sales
articles.summary: Ford Motor Co. announced plans to revive its struggling European passenger car business by building a compact Bronco SUV at its Valencia, Spain plant starting in 2028, as part of a product offensive involving five new European models by 2029. Ford will also introduce smaller electric and combustion-engine vehicles for Europe to compete with an influx of less expensive Chinese brands. Ford Pro's paid software subscriptions grew 30% year-over-year to 879,000 in Q1 2026, with gross margins above 50%, reflecting the company's pivot toward software-and-services revenue. Ford also called on the EU to align emissions regulations with consumer demand and available charging infrastructure.

articles.headline: Bond Selloff Latest: G7 Finance Ministers Discuss Debt-Market Moves
articles.summary: Bloomberg's May 18 newsletter tracked the G7 finance ministers' emergency bond market discussions in Paris as an alarming global bond selloff unfolded alongside their scheduled agenda. The gathering followed a bond market selloff triggered by fears of inflation stemming from the Iran war and the prolonged Strait of Hormuz closure. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure described the bond market as undergoing a correction rather than a collapse, while noting that public debt is no longer an irrelevant policy topic. Ministers shared views on the economic situation alongside France's broader agenda of addressing US fiscal deficits, China's trade surpluses, and European underinvestment.

articles.headline: More than 5,100 freight-related layoffs hit US supply chain sector
articles.summary: A wave of freight-related layoffs and facility closures has swept across the U.S., with more than 5,183 workers affected by shutdowns, restructurings, and contract losses tied to the logistics, manufacturing, and transportation sectors. The layoffs span at least 20 states and include warehouse operators, manufacturers, trucking companies, automotive suppliers, and food logistics providers. Major employers including FreshRealm, GEODIS, Ryder, and DSV announced mass layoffs as companies cut costs and consolidated operations. California-based FreshRealm, a ready-to-eat meal supplier for brands including Blue Apron, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and announced layoffs impacting more than 1,000 workers nationwide after disruptions tied to a 2025 listeria outbreak.

articles.headline: Transportation bill sets $240B for major modes
articles.summary: The House released a surface transportation reauthorization bill allocating $240 billion in federal spending across multiple transportation modes. The legislation covers infrastructure and services spanning a range of modal categories. The bill represents a major federal commitment to surface transportation funding as the current reauthorization period draws toward renewal.

articles.headline: Cargo theft dips in Q1, but fraud schemes surge, report says
articles.summary: Overall cargo theft declined in the first quarter, but fraud-based tactics rose sharply, according to a report by supply chain risk firm Overhaul. Deceptive pickup scams — in which thieves impersonate legitimate carriers to collect freight — climbed significantly during the period. Physical break-ins and traditional theft methods accounted for a smaller share of incidents as criminal networks shifted strategy.

articles.headline: Will the BUILD America 250 Act be the next capacity squeeze
articles.summary: The BUILD America 250 Act includes provisions that revise freight broker qualification requirements, overhaul the DataQs process for disputing safety violations, and establish a federal timeline for hair follicle drug testing of commercial drivers. The changes carry implications for broker licensing standards, motor carrier compliance obligations, and insurance renewal cycles. FreightWaves outlines how each of the three provisions could affect capacity and operational costs across the trucking and brokerage sectors.

articles.headline: Merger markup: BNSF hiked grain train charges as much as 472%, UP says in complaint
articles.summary: Union Pacific filed a formal complaint with federal regulators alleging that BNSF Railway cancelled certain reciprocal switching rates and replaced them with charges as much as 472% higher for grain shippers. UP contends the moves significantly increased shipping costs on affected routes. The complaint has been submitted to the Surface Transportation Board for review.

articles.headline: Labor Dept. jumps in on the push for driver English language proficiency
articles.summary: The U.S. Department of Labor has joined the federal government's push to enforce English language proficiency requirements for commercial truck drivers. The move adds a second federal agency to an effort that had previously been led by transportation regulators. The development signals a broadening of the enforcement framework around driver language standards.

articles.headline: This autonomous ship mooring system really sucks – and that's a good thing
articles.summary: The largest port in northern China has deployed an autonomous vacuum-based berthing system capable of securing a container ship in approximately 30 seconds. The system uses suction technology to moor vessels without traditional line-handling crews. The deployment represents an operational automation advance at one of China's major container gateway ports.

articles.headline: BUILD America 250 Act hands AV trucks a fed framework
articles.summary: The BUILD America 250 Act establishes the first federal regulatory framework for autonomous commercial trucks, though it does not authorize immediate deployment. The Department of Transportation would have two years to develop safety standards under the legislation, and liability questions would remain subject to jury determination. The bill also includes funding for workforce retraining programs tied to the transition to autonomous trucking technology.

articles.headline: Florida theft ring accused of moving $7 million in stolen goods across multiple states
articles.summary: Florida authorities arrested 14 suspects allegedly linked to an organized theft network responsible for approximately $7 million in stolen merchandise. Investigators described the group as highly organized, operating across multiple states using logistics and resale networks to move stolen goods. The arrests were the result of a multi-jurisdictional investigation into commercial cargo and retail theft.

articles.headline: AD Ports to expand Europe, Asia footprints with MBS Logistics takeover
articles.summary: Abu Dhabi's AD Ports Group is acquiring MBS Logistics in a move designed to expand its presence in European and Asian markets. The deal follows a strategy similar to that of Dubai-based DP World, which has pursued end-to-end integration across the container shipping sector. The acquisition is intended to broaden AD Ports' reach beyond its core Middle East operations.

articles.headline: 'Montgomery' ruling likely to raise pressure on trucking insurance, broker vetting
articles.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court's recent decision in the Montgomery case is expected to increase legal scrutiny of carrier selection practices and insurance coverage requirements in the trucking industry, according to attorneys who specialize in transportation law. The ruling is anticipated to raise the standard of due diligence freight brokers must apply when vetting motor carriers. Industry attorneys say the decision will likely affect both insurance renewal negotiations and broker liability exposure.

articles.headline: NAM calls for making the USMCA even more manufacturing friendly
articles.summary: The National Association of Manufacturers has called on policymakers to strengthen the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement to better support domestic manufacturing competitiveness. The NAM's recommendations focus on making the trade framework more favorable for U.S. producers ahead of the agreement's scheduled 2026 review. The group is seeking modifications that would reinforce reshoring trends and protect American manufacturing supply chains.

articles.headline: USPS to align dimensional pricing closer to FedEx, UPS
articles.summary: The U.S. Postal Service plans to revise its dimensional weight pricing methodology to more closely mirror the pricing structures used by FedEx and UPS. The change will affect how parcel rates are calculated based on package size relative to weight. The adjustment is expected to alter shipping cost calculations for e-commerce and parcel-heavy shippers that rely on USPS for last-mile delivery.

articles.headline: USPS to align dimensional pricing closer to FedEx, UPS
articles.summary: The U.S. Postal Service plans to revise its dimensional weight pricing methodology to more closely mirror the pricing structures used by FedEx and UPS. The change will affect how parcel rates are calculated based on package size relative to weight. The adjustment is expected to alter shipping cost calculations for e-commerce and parcel-heavy shippers that rely on USPS for last-mile delivery.

articles.headline: Port of Los Angeles sees April volume jump despite Iran war shadow
articles.summary: The Port of Los Angeles recorded a year-over-year increase in container volume for April, despite uncertainties stemming from the conflict involving Iran. Spring and summer cargo volumes showed strength as shippers moved goods through the port. The volume gains came amid broader concerns about potential disruptions to global shipping routes related to Middle East tensions.

articles.headline: UP, NS merger: What other railroads are saying
articles.summary: Competing railroads have begun publicly responding to the proposed merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern, with reactions ranging from competitive concern to cautious support. The consolidation would create one of the largest rail networks in North America, spanning both coasts. Other Class I carriers are weighing in as the deal advances toward federal regulatory review.

articles.headline: Product brands and the Hormuz crisis: an inventory problem
articles.summary: Consumer product brands are facing elevated inventory costs as the Strait of Hormuz crisis disrupts shipping routes and forces costly supply chain adjustments. The situation has complicated inventory management strategies for brands dependent on Middle East transit lanes. The crisis has made existing inventory imbalances more expensive to resolve as freight costs and transit times increase.

articles.headline: $6 gas and refinery fears collide with California's climate ambitions
articles.summary: California is considering providing oil refineries and other major polluters with billions of dollars in free emission allowances under its cap-and-trade program, even as the state says carbon reductions must accelerate. Two California refineries have closed in the last six months, contributing to gasoline prices reaching approximately $6 per gallon. The state faces competing pressures between maintaining fuel supply and refinery operations and meeting its climate reduction targets.

articles.headline: Avem Takes Stake in Valley Aircraft Parts Maker
articles.summary: Sun Valley-based Precision Aircraft Machining Co. Inc. (Pamco), a precision manufacturing firm serving the aerospace and defense industry, has been acquired by Avem Partners, a private equity firm. The deal gives Avem a stake in a Southern California manufacturer with established ties to the aerospace and defense sectors. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed.

articles.headline: Q1 Airports Passenger Traffic Flat
articles.summary: Cumulative passenger traffic at the four airports serving Los Angeles County was essentially flat in the first quarter of 2026, according to data released by the governing airport authorities. Approximately 20.17 million passengers traveled through the Los Angeles-area airports during the quarter. The flat passenger figures reflect subdued air travel demand across the region's major commercial aviation hubs.

articles.headline: Jurupa Valley industrial property sold
articles.summary: Bridge Logistics Properties, a national real estate investment management company, has acquired a 68-acre industrial-zoned site in Jurupa Valley, California. The purchase price was not disclosed. The property is zoned for industrial development. No additional details regarding planned development or timeline were provided in the company statement.

articles.headline: US Long Bond Yield Hits Highest Since 2023 on Inflation Concern
articles.summary: Treasuries sold off Monday, pushing the 30-year yield to its highest level since October 2023, as investor concern over accelerating inflation fueled a global debt selloff. The 30-year yield rose as much as four basis points to 5.16% as oil prices extended gains after President Trump renewed pressure on Tehran to end the Iran war. The Strait of Hormuz remains closed, with no agreement in sight between the US and Iran. Markets are pricing in no Fed rate cuts this year and increasing bets on a potential rate hike before year-end.

articles.headline: US Futures Waver as Oil Prices Edge Lower, Chips Stocks Rally
articles.summary: US futures swung to slight gains in Monday pre-market trading, erasing overnight losses as oil prices retreated from an earlier surge. S&P 500 futures rose 0.2% and Nasdaq 100 contracts gained 0.6% as of 8:54 a.m. in New York, with top semiconductor stocks including Micron Technology and Nvidia advancing. West Texas Intermediate crude oil slipped approximately 1.9% to around $103 a barrel after Iran's Tasnim reported the US had proposed a temporary waiver on oil sanctions. President Trump on Sunday said the "clock is ticking" after Iranian drones targeted a nuclear power plant in the United Arab Emirates.

articles.headline: Trump to Swear In Warsh as Fed Chair on Friday, White House Says
articles.summary: Kevin Warsh will be sworn in as Federal Reserve chair by President Donald Trump on Friday during a White House ceremony, according to a White House official. Warsh will become the central bank's 17th leader and succeed Jerome Powell, who has been serving in a temporary capacity since his official term ended the previous week. The US Senate confirmed Warsh earlier in May on a 54-45 vote, the slimmest confirmation margin ever recorded for a Fed chair. Warsh takes the helm as the central bank faces intensifying inflation driven by rising energy prices tied to the Iran war.

articles.headline: Investors Flock to Commodity ETFs (DBC) as Iran War Fuels Energy Inflation
articles.summary: Investors are pouring money into commodities funds as the US-Iran war stokes inflation, according to Invesco. Traders last week added almost $86 million to the Invesco DB Commodity Index Tracking Fund — a cross-commodities ETF with a heavy weighting toward energy — in the largest daily inflow since 2022, per Bloomberg-compiled data. The move is part of a broader surge into commodity-linked products over the past week, echoing inflow patterns that followed Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the ensuing spike in oil and natural gas prices. Diesel and energy-weighted commodities are the primary beneficiaries of the allocation shift.

articles.headline: Iran Starts Bitcoin-Backed Ship Insurance for Hormuz Strait
articles.summary: Iran has launched a Bitcoin-backed insurance service for Iranian shipping companies seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, the semi-official Fars news agency reported, citing documents from Iran's Ministry of Economy and Financial Affairs. The service, dubbed Hormuz Safe, provides Iranian shipping companies and cargo owners with what it describes as fast and verifiable digital insurance, according to a screenshot of the company's website shared by Fars. The agency did not provide a detailed breakdown of how the insurance functions or whether it is available to foreign shipping companies and vessels. The Strait of Hormuz has been largely closed amid the US-Iran conflict, choking global energy flows and driving oil prices sharply higher.

articles.headline: Samsung Strike?: Four Scenarios for the Chipmaker's Labor Dispute
articles.summary: Samsung Electronics and its largest labor union are locked in talks to avert a strike at the world's largest memory chip maker, with the potential for significant disruption to semiconductor supply chains if a work stoppage proceeds. The dispute involves approximately 47,000 workers and centers on bonus distribution, according to reports. The talks come at a delicate moment for Samsung, which has been recording strong profits driven by red-hot demand for AI chips and faces fierce competition from SK Hynix and Micron Technology. A strike could further elevate already high chip prices and affect technology supply chains from smartphones to servers.

articles.headline: Ford in Talks to Supply Military Trucks in Europe, North America
articles.summary: Ford Motor Co. is in negotiations with defense departments in Europe and North America to supply pickup trucks and software to their armed forces, the automaker confirmed Monday in a blog post. The talks, which began last year, are described as "productive" but have not yet yielded a contract. Chief Executive Officer Jim Farley told analysts last month that Ford is in "early discussions with the US government on some defense related needs." The move signals Ford's push into defense contracting as a new revenue stream amid the ongoing Iran conflict's effects on global auto and manufacturing demand.

articles.headline: White House Details Trump-Xi Summit Trade Commitments: China to Buy $17 Billion in U.S. Agricultural Goods Annually Through 2028
articles.summary: The White House on Sunday released details of trade understandings reached during President Trump's two-day state visit to Beijing, saying China agreed to purchase at least $17 billion per year in U.S. agricultural products — including beef and poultry — for 2026, 2027, and 2028. China will restore market access for U.S. beef and resume poultry imports from states certified bird-flu-free by the USDA. The agreement builds on a prior soybean purchase commitment from October 2025, under which China agreed to buy 25 million metric tons annually for three years. China's imports of U.S. agricultural goods fell from a peak of $38 billion in 2022 to $8 billion in 2025, according to USDA data cited in Reuters reporting.

articles.headline: Trump-Xi Summit Produced 'Modest' Commercial Commitments With Major Disputes Unresolved, Reuters Reports
articles.summary: Reuters reporters Michael Martina, David Brunnstrom, David Lawder, and Mei Mei Chu reported that President Trump's Beijing summit with Xi Jinping produced modest commercial and trade commitments but no public Chinese commitment to help end the Iran war. Disputes over Beijing's trade practices, military posture, and technology access were described as largely unresolved. Both sides framed the outcomes as preliminary, with China's Ministry of Commerce calling for continued negotiations on tariff reductions and market access issues. The two leaders agreed to meet again in the U.S. in September.

articles.headline: Trump-Xi Summit Produced 'Modest' Commercial Commitments With Major Disputes Unresolved, Reuters Reports
articles.summary: Reuters reporters Michael Martina, David Brunnstrom, David Lawder, and Mei Mei Chu reported that President Trump's Beijing summit with Xi Jinping produced modest commercial and trade commitments but no public Chinese commitment to help end the Iran war. Disputes over Beijing's trade practices, military posture, and technology access were described as largely unresolved. Both sides framed the outcomes as preliminary, with China's Ministry of Commerce calling for continued negotiations on tariff reductions and market access issues. The two leaders agreed to meet again in the U.S. in September.

articles.headline: Iran War, Hormuz Closure Drive Up Energy and Shipping Costs Across Airlines, Chemicals, Autos — Reuters
articles.summary: Reuters reported that companies across multiple sectors have cited higher energy and shipping costs, supply-chain disruptions, production cuts, dividend suspensions, furloughs, fuel surcharges, and emergency government-assistance requests as a result of the ongoing Iran war and Strait of Hormuz closure. Airlines, chemicals, consumer goods, oil and gas, and automotive companies are among the hardest hit. Europe and Asia are described as especially exposed to higher oil prices and disrupted Middle East trade routes. The U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, in effect since April 13, has contributed to the virtual closure of a waterway that previously carried roughly 27% of the world's seaborne crude oil trade.

articles.headline: White House touts deals on soybeans and rare earths after Trump-Xi summit, while China talks up tariff cuts
articles.summary: The White House released details of agreements reached at the Trump-Xi Beijing summit, including China's commitment to purchase at least $17 billion per year in U.S. agricultural products through 2028 and an initial order of 200 Boeing aircraft for Chinese airlines. The U.S. and China agreed to establish a Board of Trade and a Board of Investment to manage bilateral economic relations. China indicated reducing tariffs would be part of the plans, while the U.S. readout did not mention duties. Both sides characterized the summit outcomes as 'preliminary,' with further negotiations expected in coming weeks and months.

articles.headline: From a 'board of trade' to Boeing planes, what did Xi and Trump actually agree to?
articles.summary: Following the Trump-Xi summit in Beijing, China agreed to purchase $17 billion annually in U.S. agricultural goods plus 25 million metric tons of soybeans — totaling roughly $27 billion per year — and to restore market access for U.S. beef and resume poultry imports. China also agreed to 'address U.S. concerns' over supply chain shortages of rare earths including yttrium, scandium, neodymium, and indium, though Beijing's statement did not explicitly confirm this. The White House cited China's initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft, which Boeing has not yet publicly confirmed; China confirmed only aircraft procurement arrangements.

articles.headline: Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Secures Historic Deals with China, Delivering for American Workers, Farmers, and Industry
articles.summary: The White House fact sheet details agreements from the Trump-Xi summit, including China's commitment to purchase at least $17 billion per year in U.S. agricultural products in 2026, 2027, and 2028. China approved an initial purchase of 200 American-made Boeing aircraft, the first Chinese commitment to Boeing aircraft since 2017. China will address U.S. concerns regarding supply chain shortages related to rare earths and critical minerals including yttrium, scandium, neodymium, and indium. The two countries established a U.S.-China Board of Trade and a U.S.-China Board of Investment as the 'cornerstone' of the agreement.

articles.headline: Trump-Xi summit: China agrees to boost trade for U.S. beef, poultry
articles.summary: China agreed at the Trump-Xi summit to purchase $17 billion per year in U.S. agricultural products through 2028 and order 200 Boeing aircraft, a figure analysts described as fewer than expected, causing Boeing shares to fall. China also renewed market access for U.S. beef by restoring listings for more than 400 U.S. beef facilities and resumed poultry imports from states certified free of bird flu. The 'cornerstone' of the agreement is a board of trade mechanism that could allow tariff reductions on some $30 billion in non-sensitive goods. Analysts said Trump laid 'solid groundwork' but several issues remain unresolved, including Taiwan and Iran.

articles.headline: Appeals Court Keeps Section 122 Tariffs In Place (For Now): What Importers Need To Know
articles.source: Mondaq / Customs & International Trade Law Blog
articles.summary: On May 7, 2026, the U.S. Court of International Trade ruled that the Trump Administration's 10% global tariffs imposed under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 were unlawful, issuing a permanent injunction for three named plaintiffs — the State of Washington, Burlap & Barrel, and Basic Fun. On May 12, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit entered an administrative stay, suspending the CIT's ruling while the appeal proceeds, meaning Section 122 tariffs remain in effect for all other importers. Importers paid an estimated $25 billion in Section 122 duties since February 24, 2026. The tariffs are currently set to expire July 24, 2026, but the administration may impose replacement tariffs under Section 301 or Section 232.

articles.headline: Amazon and Walmart's $1 trillion battle to win rural America's shoppers
articles.summary: Amazon and Walmart are competing to serve rural U.S. consumers through expanded last-mile delivery infrastructure, a market analysts at Morgan Stanley estimate could generate up to $1 trillion in annual sales. Amazon is establishing small delivery hubs serving clusters of neighboring towns, with the goal of cutting delivery times from up to five days to under two days, according to Holly Sullivan, Amazon's vice president of worldwide economic development. Approximately 90% of Americans live within 10 miles of a Walmart location, and 45% of its full-service Supercenters are in areas with populations under 20,000, giving Walmart a proximity advantage. FedEx, UPS, and the U.S. Postal Service are simultaneously reducing or slowing deliveries to certain rural locations to cut costs.

articles.headline: Could new Zim offer start bidding war?
articles.summary: An investor has submitted a surprise bid for ZIM Integrated Shipping Services that would increase the purchase price and keep the Israeli ocean carrier under Israeli control. The unsolicited offer raises the possibility of a bidding war for the liner. No financial terms of the competing bid were disclosed in the report.

articles.headline: Software vendor offers proposal to establish detention, demurrage accountability
articles.summary: A beneficial cargo owner technology provider has proposed a framework identifying 20 use cases under which shippers, consignees, and carriers can be held accountable for container detention and demurrage charges. The proposal is aimed at reducing costly dispute resolution between supply chain parties. The vendor's framework seeks to establish clear standards for assigning responsibility for container storage costs.

articles.headline: Guangzhou begins work on $2 billion fifth development phase at Nansha port
articles.summary: Construction has begun on a $2 billion fifth development phase at Nansha port in Guangzhou, China. The project includes four berths capable of handling vessels exceeding 21,000 TEUs, along with 15 berths for regional feeder vessels. The expansion represents a significant addition to one of China's major container port facilities.

articles.headline: US and China to establish trade board, tout agriculture commitments
articles.summary: The United States and China have announced plans to establish a trade board as part of ongoing bilateral trade negotiations. The two countries also highlighted agriculture commitments as part of the framework. Further details on the structure and scope of the trade board were included in the agreement announcement.

articles.headline: Parcel express services evolve as market fragmentation accelerates
articles.summary: Andy Dyer, CEO of transportation management firm AFS, which manages approximately $3 billion in parcel spend annually for its clients, says the parcel carrier market is experiencing accelerating fragmentation. Dyer notes the sector has undergone numerous disruptions, evolutions, and reinventions in recent years. The report examines how express parcel services are adapting to a market increasingly characterized by multiple competing carriers.

articles.headline: Industrial Realty Group, Sachem Capital Merge to Form $3.4B Industrial REIT
articles.summary: Industrial Realty Group (IRG), one of the largest private owners of U.S. industrial real estate, has agreed to merge with public mortgage trust Sachem Capital to form IRG Realty Trust, a $3.4 billion publicly traded real estate investment trust. The combined entity will bring together IRG's private industrial portfolio with Sachem Capital's public market structure. The merger creates a new publicly traded industrial REIT with a combined asset value of $3.4 billion.

articles.headline: Bond Traders See Shift Toward New Era of Higher Yields
articles.summary: A new era of elevated borrowing costs is potentially underway as war-driven inflation angst intensifies in the US bond market, sending 30-year yields toward a two-decade high above 5%, Bloomberg reported. Treasuries extended their slide Monday in Asia after their worst week in a year, with a renewed rally in oil adding to worries from reports showing inflation accelerated last month. The fear of resurgent price pressures roiled fixed-income globally, sparking a rout in markets including the UK and Japan. G-7 finance chiefs are set to discuss the debt selloff at their Paris meeting.

articles.headline: Latest Iran Offer on War Is Not Enough, Says White House
articles.summary: Hopes for a breakthrough in the US-Iran standoff over the closure of the Strait of Hormuz were dashed again on Monday after Iran delivered an updated peace proposal that the White House deemed insufficient. Earlier reports of a potential deal had fueled market optimism, but Wall Street's rebound attempt failed as stocks fell and Brent crude topped $110 per barrel in a volatile session. The S&P 500 erased earlier gains as oil extended its advance. The Strait of Hormuz has remained largely blocked since late February, cutting roughly 20% of global seaborne oil trade.

articles.headline: Oil Slips as Trump Spurs Optimism Over Iran Deal: Markets Wrap
articles.summary: Oil dropped in early Asia trading after President Donald Trump said he was holding off on fresh military strikes against Iran following appeals from Persian Gulf allies, boosting hopes for a deal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to energy flows. West Texas Intermediate crude fell 1.4% after Trump said plans for a strike were called off, with the president adding that "serious negotiations are now taking place." S&P 500 futures were steady after the benchmark index had nearly wiped out its losses in a choppy Monday session. The Strait of Hormuz has remained largely closed since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in late February.

articles.headline: Oil Extends Gains as Trump Says Clock Is Ticking for Iran Deal
articles.summary: Oil rose for a third consecutive day on Monday as the US and Iran remained far apart on a deal to end weeks of war and reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude advanced above $110 a barrel, after adding almost 8% the prior week, while West Texas Intermediate rose above $107. President Trump posted on social media that "For Iran, the Clock is Ticking, and they better get moving, FAST," signaling his patience with Tehran was wearing thin. The International Energy Agency cautioned that oil inventories globally are depleting at a record pace as Hormuz remains closed.

articles.headline: LIRR Strike Inches Toward a Fourth Day as Talks Progress Slowly
articles.summary: The Long Island Rail Road strike approached a fourth day on Monday as labor groups and transit officials had yet to reach a deal, leaving the nation's busiest commuter rail line shuttered for the evening commute. Roughly 3,500 engineers, signalmen and electrical workers walked off the job on Saturday after negotiations between the state-run Metropolitan Transportation Authority and five union coalition members collapsed over wages and healthcare premiums. Parties restarted negotiations Sunday after failing to reach a deal by a late Friday deadline. The shutdown is the first LIRR work stoppage in more than 30 years, affecting over 250,000 daily commuters.

articles.headline: LIRR Strike Jams Roads, Prompts Long Commutes as Talks Continue
articles.summary: Long Island workers making their way into New York City grappled with long commutes Monday as the Long Island Rail Road entered its third strike day, the first weekday of the work stoppage. The LIRR — the nation's busiest commuter railroad — halted service on Saturday after roughly 3,500 engineers, signalmen and electrical workers walked off the job following a stalemate between the Metropolitan Transportation Authority and union leaders. Roads and alternative transit were strained across the region as commuters scrambled for substitute transportation options. The National Mediation Board, which governs labor relations for railroads, had stepped in to summon parties to negotiations in Manhattan.

articles.headline: US Premarket Movers for May 18, 2026
articles.summary: S&P 500 Index futures fell 0.4% as of 7:37 a.m. New York time on Monday as investors watched bond markets to see if Friday's surge in yields to multi-year highs would extend. The premarket session tracked the prior week's major bond selloff driven by accelerating inflation data and oil price gains tied to the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz disruption. Bloomberg reported on the biggest US movers before the opening bell in a volatile market session dominated by energy and rate concerns.

articles.headline: US Premarket Movers for May 18, 2026
articles.summary: S&P 500 Index futures fell 0.4% as of 7:37 a.m. New York time on Monday as investors watched bond markets to see if Friday's surge in yields to multi-year highs would extend. The premarket session tracked the prior week's major bond selloff driven by accelerating inflation data and oil price gains tied to the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz disruption. Bloomberg reported on the biggest US movers before the opening bell in a volatile market session dominated by energy and rate concerns.

articles.headline: US Lawmakers Plan New $130 Fee for Electric Vehicle Owners
articles.summary: House lawmakers released a massive $580 billion transportation bill Sunday that would impose new annual fees on electric and hybrid vehicles as gasoline prices surge following the Iran war. The bipartisan legislation, released by members of the House transportation committee, would impose an annual registration fee of $130 per electric vehicle, gradually rising biennially to $150, and as much as $50 for hybrids. The fees are intended to help fund the Highway Trust Fund as EV adoption reduces gasoline tax revenues. The legislation represents the first major federal transportation funding overhaul in years.

articles.headline: Kioxia's Booming Shares Head for Liquidity Boost With US Float
articles.summary: Kioxia Holdings Corp. announced plans to float American Depositary Shares on a US stock exchange, aiming to expand its investor base amid global fervor over memory chips. The Japanese chipmaker said in a release that the move would help raise corporate value, though details including the schedule and method remain undetermined and the company may not ultimately pursue the listing. ADSs would make shares directly available for trading, reducing arbitrage costs compared to depositary receipts that Kioxia already offers. The announcement positions Kioxia to capitalize on surging chip demand driven by AI infrastructure investment.

articles.headline: West Marine Files Chapter 11 Bankruptcy to Cut Debt, Close More Stores
articles.summary: Boating supply retailer West Marine Inc. filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on May 17 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, citing weaker sales as consumers pull back on outdoor recreation due to inflation and severe weather. The company reached a restructuring support agreement with 96.2% of term loan lenders, 100% of FILO lenders, and 93.9% of equity holders to either find a buyer or hand control to lenders owed $251 million. Approximately 200 stores across 34 states and Puerto Rico will remain open during restructuring. CEO Paulee Day said the company will "optimize our operations and rationalize our footprint" as part of the process.

articles.headline: Oil Climbs as Iran War Shows No Sign of Ending; Stocks Waver on Deal Doubts
articles.summary: Wall Street's rebound attempt failed Monday as oil rose after Iranian media reported fundamental differences remain in U.S.-Iran negotiations, with Tehran citing "excessive demands and unrealistic positions" in the latest U.S. draft proposal. U.S. crude topped $106 per barrel in volatile trading while Brent crude gained over 1.9% to $111.34 per barrel. The S&P 500 dropped 0.07% and the Nasdaq slid 0.51%, with traders monitoring oil prices and bond yields. President Trump warned Iran on Sunday that "the Clock is Ticking," adding to market anxiety over Strait of Hormuz shipping disruption.

articles.headline: China's Economy Loses Steam in April as Retail Sales Hit 40-Month Low
articles.summary: China's retail sales rose only 0.2% in April from a year ago, the weakest growth since December 2022, as the fallout from the Iran war dampened momentum in the world's second-largest economy. Industrial output climbed 4.1% in April, undershooting expectations for a 5.9% rise, while urban fixed asset investment contracted 1.6% against expectations for 1.6% growth. Crude oil refining volumes fell 5.8% from a year earlier, the steepest decline since August 2024. Following the Trump-Xi Beijing summit, China agreed to purchase at least $17 billion per year in U.S. agricultural products in 2026 through 2028, and an initial 200 jets from Boeing.

articles.headline: Pet Supplies Plus Franchisee PSP TS LLC Files Chapter 11 Bankruptcy
articles.summary: Florida-based Pet Supplies Plus franchisee PSP TS LLC filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Middle District of Florida in Tampa on May 12, listing $100,000 to $500,000 in assets and $1 million to $10 million in liabilities. The Holiday, Fla.-based franchisee's single Pet Supplies Plus store remains open, and the Pet Supplies Plus franchisor itself has not filed for bankruptcy. The Livonia, Mich.-based Pet Supplies Plus chain operates 725 locations in 44 states and 26 Wag N' Wash facilities nationwide. The debtor did not indicate a specific reason for the filing.

articles.headline: Industrial Realty Group Takes Portfolio Public
articles.summary: Los Angeles-based Industrial Realty Group is combining 98 industrial properties into a new publicly traded REIT through a definitive contribution agreement with Connecticut-based mortgage lender Sachem Capital Corp., creating IRG Realty Trust with an implied enterprise value of approximately $3.4 billion. The combined entity is expected to rank among the top 10 publicly listed industrial REITs by enterprise value, with IRG owning approximately 94.1% of the new company via operating partnership units and existing Sachem shareholders retaining roughly 5.9%. The 98 properties — described as mission-critical industrial infrastructure leased to manufacturing, distribution, and logistics tenants — carry a gross real estate asset value of $2.9 billion; Sachem's approximately $470 million in existing mortgage loan assets will also be included. The transaction, unanimously approved by Sachem's board, is expected to close by end of 2026 subject to Sachem shareholder approval, with Scotiabank advising IRG and Piper Sandler advising Sachem.

articles.headline: 2026 Iran war fuel crisis — Strait of Hormuz closure: ongoing global shipping and energy disruption
articles.source: Wikipedia (citing IEA, CRS, Dallas Fed, UNCTAD)
articles.summary: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which approximately 20% of global oil trade passes, has caused what the IEA characterized as the 'largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.' Iranian forces declared the Strait closed beginning March 4, 2026, following the U.S.-Israeli Operation Epic Fury launched February 28; a brief reopening April 21–22 collapsed within 24 hours. Brent crude prices have exceeded $90 per barrel, container shipping companies including Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd suspended Mideast routes, and Asia-to-U.S. East Coast transpacific rates have climbed to approximately $3,800/FEU as of May 12, 2026, per SCFI data.

articles.headline: NerdWallet economic outlook week of May 18: Inflation risks tipping as CPI and PPI data signal continued price pressure
articles.summary: NerdWallet senior economist Elizabeth Renter noted that this week's CPI and PPI data signal risks tilting toward inflation, with the oil price shock described as 'significant, and only beginning.' Both sides of the Fed's dual mandate — stable prices and full employment — have been at risk, but current data show inflationary pressures strengthening. The U.S. trade deficit stood at $60.3 billion in March 2026, up 4.4% from February, with imports reaching $381.2 billion and exports $320.9 billion per BEA data.

articles.headline: Trump talks up trade deals with China, but experts see no big wins for U.S.
articles.summary: Analysts and former trade negotiators assessed the Trump-Xi Beijing summit as falling short of a major breakthrough despite White House claims of 'fantastic trade deals.' China agreed to purchase at least $17 billion in U.S. agricultural products over three years and restored market access for hundreds of U.S. beef facilities, according to the White House fact sheet. China also agreed to address U.S. access concerns for rare earths and other critical minerals, while industries have continued to struggle with supply shortages since Beijing postponed sweeping rare earth controls in October 2025. Boeing shares fell 3.8% on Friday, reflecting investor disappointment that the aircraft order of 200 jets was smaller than pre-summit expectations.
